claim: Animals can continuously learn different tasks to adapt to changing environments.
source: Animals can continuously learn different tasks to adapt to changing environments and, therefore, have strategies to effectively cope with inter-task interference, including both proactive interference (Pro-I) and retroactive interference (Retro-I).
evidence: This is a general statement about animal learning capabilities presented in the abstract without specific experimental data in this manuscript.

claim: Animals have strategies to effectively cope with inter-task interference, including both proactive interference (Pro-I) and retroactive interference (Retro-I).
source: Animals can continuously learn different tasks to adapt to changing environments and, therefore, have strategies to effectively cope with inter-task interference, including both proactive interference (Pro-I) and retroactive interference (Retro-I).
evidence: This is a general statement about animal learning capabilities presented in the abstract.

claim: Many biological mechanisms are known to contribute to learning, memory, and forgetting for a single task.
source: Many biological mechanisms are known to contribute to learning, memory, and forgetting for a single task, however, mechanisms involved only when learning sequential different tasks are relatively poorly understood.
evidence: This statement references existing knowledge in the field without specific citations in this sentence.

claim: Mechanisms involved only when learning sequential different tasks are relatively poorly understood.
source: Many biological mechanisms are known to contribute to learning, memory, and forgetting for a single task, however, mechanisms involved only when learning sequential different tasks are relatively poorly understood.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: Pro-I is more sensitive to an inter-task interval (ITI) than Retro-I.
source: Pro-I is more sensitive to an inter-task interval (ITI) than Retro-I.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-E comparing Pro-I and Retro-I at different ITIs.

claim: Pro-I and Retro-I occur together at short ITI (<20 min).
source: They occur together at short ITI (<20 min), while only Retro-I remains significant at ITI beyond 20 min.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2 showing both types of interference at short intervals.

claim: Only Retro-I remains significant at ITI beyond 20 min.
source: They occur together at short ITI (<20 min), while only Retro-I remains significant at ITI beyond 20 min.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2 showing persistence of Retro-I but not Pro-I at longer intervals.

claim: Acutely overexpressing Corkscrew (CSW) in mushroom body (MB) neurons reduces Pro-I.
source: Acutely overexpressing Corkscrew (CSW), an evolutionarily conserved protein tyrosine phosphatase SHP2, in mushroom body (MB) neurons reduces Pro-I, whereas acute knockdown of CSW exacerbates Pro-I.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3D, E, and H showing reduced Pro-I with CSW overexpression.

claim: CSW is an evolutionarily conserved protein tyrosine phosphatase SHP2.
source: Acutely overexpressing Corkscrew (CSW), an evolutionarily conserved protein tyrosine phosphatase SHP2, in mushroom body (MB) neurons reduces Pro-I, whereas acute knockdown of CSW exacerbates Pro-I.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the identity and conservation of CSW.

claim: Acute knockdown of CSW exacerbates Pro-I.
source: Acutely overexpressing Corkscrew (CSW), an evolutionarily conserved protein tyrosine phosphatase SHP2, in mushroom body (MB) neurons reduces Pro-I, whereas acute knockdown of CSW exacerbates Pro-I.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3A, B, and C showing increased Pro-I with CSW knockdown.

claim: The function of CSW in regulating Pro-I relies on the γ subset of MB neurons.
source: Such function of CSW is further found to rely on the γ subset of MB neurons and the downstream Raf/MAPK pathway.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3G, H, and I showing CSW effects specifically in γ neurons.

claim: The function of CSW in regulating Pro-I relies on the downstream Raf/MAPK pathway.
source: Such function of CSW is further found to rely on the γ subset of MB neurons and the downstream Raf/MAPK pathway.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing that Raf/MAPK pathway components regulate Pro-I and that Raf acts downstream of CSW.

claim: Manipulating CSW does not affect Retro-I.
source: In contrast, manipulating CSW does not affect Retro-I as well as a single learning task.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3F showing no effect of CSW manipulation on Retro-I.

claim: Manipulating CSW does not affect a single learning task.
source: In contrast, manipulating CSW does not affect Retro-I as well as a single learning task.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C showing no effect on single-task learning and memory.

claim: Manipulation of Rac1 regulates Retro-I.
source: Interestingly, manipulation of Rac1, a molecule that regulates Retro-I, does not affect Pro-I.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2F showing that Rac1 manipulation affects Retro-I.

claim: Manipulation of Rac1 does not affect Pro-I.
source: Interestingly, manipulation of Rac1, a molecule that regulates Retro-I, does not affect Pro-I.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2F showing no effect of Rac1 manipulation on Pro-I.

claim: Learning different tasks consecutively triggers distinct molecular mechanisms to tune proactive and retroactive interference.
source: Thus, our findings suggest that learning different tasks consecutively triggers distinct molecular mechanisms to tune proactive and retroactive interference.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from the differential effects of CSW on Pro-I vs Retro-I and Rac1 on Retro-I vs Pro-I.

claim: Continual learning is a natural ability of animals ranging from invertebrates to vertebrates.
source: Continual learning is a natural ability of animals ranging from invertebrates to vertebrates but a great challenge for artificial intelligence (Fayek et al., 2020; Kudithipudi et al., 2022; Parisi et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Continual learning is a great challenge for artificial intelligence.
source: Continual learning is a natural ability of animals ranging from invertebrates to vertebrates but a great challenge for artificial intelligence (Fayek et al., 2020; Kudithipudi et al., 2022; Parisi et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature on AI and continual learning.

claim: The interference from the previous task on the learning and memory of the current task is called Pro-I.
source: The interference from the previous task on the learning and memory of the current task is called Pro-I, while the interference from the current task on the memory of the following task is named Retro-I (Bouton, 1993; Miller, 2021; Wixted, 2004).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The interference from the current task on the memory of the following task is named Retro-I.
source: The interference from the previous task on the learning and memory of the current task is called Pro-I, while the interference from the current task on the memory of the following task is named Retro-I (Bouton, 1993; Miller, 2021; Wixted, 2004).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: We have much understanding of the molecular mechanisms of learning and memory for a single learning task.
source: Although, we have much understanding of the molecular mechanisms of learning and memory for a single learning task (Johansen et al., 2011; Kandel et al., 2014), the molecular mechanisms that modulate the interferences between different tasks remain unclear.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature on learning and memory mechanisms.

claim: The molecular mechanisms that modulate the interferences between different tasks remain unclear.
source: Although, we have much understanding of the molecular mechanisms of learning and memory for a single learning task (Johansen et al., 2011; Kandel et al., 2014), the molecular mechanisms that modulate the interferences between different tasks remain unclear.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that motivates the current study.

claim: Drosophila is a well-studied and highly tractable genetic model organism for understanding molecular mechanisms underlying a single learning task.
source: Drosophila is a well-studied and highly tractable genetic model organism for understanding molecular mechanisms underlying a single learning task (Davis, 2005; Noyes et al., 2021; Waddell and Quinn, 2001) as well as related human diseases (Mariano et al., 2020; Pandey and Nichols, 2011; van Alphen and van Swinderen, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature on Drosophila as a model organism.

claim: Drosophila is a model organism for studying related human diseases.
source: Drosophila is a well-studied and highly tractable genetic model organism for understanding molecular mechanisms underlying a single learning task (Davis, 2005; Noyes et al., 2021; Waddell and Quinn, 2001) as well as related human diseases (Mariano et al., 2020; Pandey and Nichols, 2011; van Alphen and van Swinderen, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature on Drosophila disease models.

claim: Drosophila has emerged as an excellent model for studying interference mechanisms between two associative learning tasks.
source: In recent years, Drosophila has also emerged as an excellent model for studying interference mechanisms between two associative learning tasks.
evidence: This statement is supported by the subsequent citations to studies on interference in Drosophila.

claim: Several molecules, including Rac1, Foraging, Scribble, SLC22A, Fmr1, SCAR, and Dia, have been reported to regulate Retro-I.
source: Several molecules, including Rac1, Foraging, Scribble, SLC22A, Fmr1, SCAR, and Dia, have been reported to regulate Retro-I (Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2016; Dong et al., 2016; Gai et al., 2016; Gao et al., 2019; Reaume et al., 2011; Shuai et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies identifying these molecules.

claim: Scribble and SLC22A have been reported to regulate Pro-I.
source: Of these molecules, Scribble and SLC22A, have also been reported to regulate Pro-I (Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2016; Gai et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Retro-I and Pro-I may have shared regulatory molecules.
source: It indicates that Retro-I and Pro-I may have shared regulatory molecules.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Scribble and SLC22A regulate both types of interference.

claim: Resistance to Pro-I and Retro-I is very different in patients with autism.
source: Previous studies reported that resistance to Pro-I and Retro-I is very different in patients with autism (Mottron et al., 1998), schizophrenia (Torres et al., 2001), and ADHD (Orban et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Resistance to Pro-I and Retro-I is very different in patients with schizophrenia.
source: Previous studies reported that resistance to Pro-I and Retro-I is very different in patients with autism (Mottron et al., 1998), schizophrenia (Torres et al., 2001), and ADHD (Orban et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Resistance to Pro-I and Retro-I is very different in patients with ADHD.
source: Previous studies reported that resistance to Pro-I and Retro-I is very different in patients with autism (Mottron et al., 1998), schizophrenia (Torres et al., 2001), and ADHD (Orban et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Pro-I and Retro-I may have distinct molecular mechanisms.
source: It raises a possibility that Pro-I and Retro-I may have distinct molecular mechanisms.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential resistance patterns in clinical populations.

claim: All reported molecules in regulating Retro-I or Pro-I also play important roles in the learning or memory of a single learning task.
source: Of note, all reported molecules in regulating Retro-I or Pro-I also play important roles in the learning or memory of a single learning task (Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2016; Dong et al., 2016; Gai et al., 2016; Gao et al., 2019; Reaume et al., 2011; Shuai et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Pro-I is closely related to content similarity, context similarity, and the time interval between the proactive task and the target task.
source: Psychological studies have shown that Pro-I is closely related to content similarity, context similarity, and the time interval between the proactive task and the target task (Kliegl and Bäuml, 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to psychological studies.

claim: An aversive associative learning task produces significant Pro-I on another similar task immediately following in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, it has been known that an aversive associative learning task produces significant Pro-I on another similar task immediately following (Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2016; Gai et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous Drosophila studies.

claim: Significant Pro-I was observed between two consecutive aversive tasks.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2016; Gai et al., 2016), significant Pro-I was observed between two consecutive aversive tasks (Figure 1A; Associative group).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: Pro-I phenomenon was still evident 1 hr later.
source: This Pro-I phenomenon was still evident 1 hr later (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and was not affected by changing the order of the two tasks (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Pro-I was not affected by changing the order of the two tasks.
source: This Pro-I phenomenon was still evident 1 hr later (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and was not affected by changing the order of the two tasks (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: No significant Pro-I was observed when the proactive task was changed into non-associative stimuli.
source: With such changes, no significant Pro-I was observed (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A comparing associative vs non-associative proactive tasks.

claim: No significant Pro-I was observed when the proactive task was changed into an appetitive learning task.
source: With such changes, no significant Pro-I was observed (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B comparing aversive vs appetitive proactive tasks.

claim: When both tasks were learned in the same context, the Pro-I was evident.
source: When both tasks were learned in the same context, the Pro-I was evident. In contrast, when the two tasks were learned in different contexts, the Pro-I was no longer observed.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C comparing same vs different context conditions.

claim: When the two tasks were learned in different contexts, the Pro-I was no longer observed.
source: When both tasks were learned in the same context, the Pro-I was evident. In contrast, when the two tasks were learned in different contexts, the Pro-I was no longer observed.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C comparing same vs different context conditions.

claim: A single aversive learning task can produce two opposing memory components: avoidance memory and approach memory.
source: In addition, recent studies have found that a single aversive learning task can produce two opposing memory components: avoidance memory and approach memory (Jacob and Waddell, 2020; Naganos et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Pro-I only affected avoidance memory.
source: Here, we found that the Pro-I only affected avoidance memory (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Reducing inter-task similarity by changing learning content or context can release Pro-I in Drosophila.
source: Together, these data suggest that reducing inter-task similarity by changing learning content or context can release Pro-I in Drosophila, which is consistent with psychological studies (Kliegl and Bäuml, 2021).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results in Figure 1 and is consistent with cited psychological studies.

claim: Flies showed significant Pro-I when the ITI was 15 min or less (0, 5, 10, and 15 min).
source: Flies showed significant Pro-I when the ITI was 15 min or less (0, 5, 10, and 15 min).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: If the ITI was 20 min or more (20, 30, and 60 min), no significant Pro-I was observed.
source: If the ITI was 20 min or more (20, 30, and 60 min), no significant Pro-I was observed.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: When the ITI was gradually increased from 0 to 60 min (0, 20, 30, and 60 min), the flies consistently exhibited significant Retro-I.
source: In contrast, when the ITI was gradually increased from 0 to 60 min (0, 20, 30, and 60 min), the flies consistently exhibited significant Retro-I (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: The result on Retro-I is consistent with previous studies.
source: This result is consistent with previous studies on Retro-I (Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2016; Dong et al., 2016; Gai et al., 2016; Gao et al., 2019; Reaume et al., 2011; Shuai et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement compares current findings to previous literature.

claim: Rac1 is required to mediate Retro-I when the ITI is 1.5 hr.
source: Rac1 is required to mediate Retro-I when the ITI is 1.5 hr (Shuai et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Acute manipulation of Rac1 activity in mushroom body (MB) neurons is sufficient to regulate memory performance.
source: Since acute manipulation of Rac1 activity in mushroom body (MB) neurons is sufficient to regulate memory performance (Gao et al., 2019; Shuai et al., 2010), Rac1 transgenes were expressed using MB-GS, a Gene-Switch (GS) tool capable of inducing transgene expression specifically in the MB only on administration of the drug RU486 (Mao et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Suppressing Rac1 activity in MB neurons significantly mitigated the Retro-I.
source: Suppressing (MB-GS/UAS-Rac1-DN, RU486+) or increasing (MB-GS/UAS-Rac1-CA, RU486+) Rac1 activity in MB neurons significantly mitigated or aggravated the Retro-I, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Increasing Rac1 activity in MB neurons significantly aggravated the Retro-I.
source: Suppressing (MB-GS/UAS-Rac1-DN, RU486+) or increasing (MB-GS/UAS-Rac1-CA, RU486+) Rac1 activity in MB neurons significantly mitigated or aggravated the Retro-I, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Manipulations of Rac1 activity did not affect the Pro-I.
source: However, the same manipulations did not affect the Pro-I, indicating that there is a different molecular mechanism underlying the Pro-I.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: There is a different molecular mechanism underlying the Pro-I compared to Retro-I.
source: However, the same manipulations did not affect the Pro-I, indicating that there is a different molecular mechanism underlying the Pro-I.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of Rac1 manipulation on Pro-I vs Retro-I.

claim: CSW has been reported to regulate the 'time interval' effect in long-term memory (LTM) formation in Drosophila.
source: Given that CSW, an evolutionarily conserved protein tyrosine phosphatase SHP2, has been reported to regulate the 'time interval' effect in long-term memory (LTM) formation in Drosophila (Pagani et al., 2009), we tested the role of CSW in Pro-I.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Acutely knocking down CSW in MB neurons using two independent RNAi lines showed more severe Pro-I.
source: Compared to the parental control group (MB-GS/+, RU486+), acutely knocking down CSW in MB neurons using two independent RNAi lines (MB-GS/UAS-csw-RNAi-1 and MB-GS/UAS-csw-RNAi-2; RU486+) showed more severe Pro-I, which can be better reflected by the Pro-I+/Pro-I– ratio (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Pro-I was no longer observed in control flies when the ITI was 20 min.
source: When the ITI was 20 min, Pro-I was no longer observed in control flies but was still present in flies with acute knockdown of CSW (Figure 3C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Pro-I was still present in flies with acute knockdown of CSW when the ITI was 20 min.
source: When the ITI was 20 min, Pro-I was no longer observed in control flies but was still present in flies with acute knockdown of CSW (Figure 3C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Acute overexpression of CSW in MB neurons reduced Pro-I.
source: Conversely, acute overexpression of CSW in MB neurons (MB-GS/UAS-csw, RU486+) reduced Pro-I by using a newly constructed transgenic strain (Figure 3D and E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and E) and a previously reported strain (Botham et al., 2008; Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D, E and supplementary figures.

claim: Bidirectional manipulation of CSW expression in MB neurons did not affect Retro-I.
source: Of note, bidirectional manipulation of CSW expression in MB neurons did not affect Retro-I (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The MB contains ~2000 intrinsic neurons called Kenyon cells (KCs).
source: The MB contains ~2000 intrinsic neurons called Kenyon cells (KCs), which are further divided into three major types: γ neurons (~675), α/β neurons (~990), and α'/β'neurons (~350) (Aso et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to a previous study on MB anatomy.

claim: Kenyon cells are divided into three major types: γ neurons (~675), α/β neurons (~990), and α'/β'neurons (~350).
source: The MB contains ~2000 intrinsic neurons called Kenyon cells (KCs), which are further divided into three major types: γ neurons (~675), α/β neurons (~990), and α'/β'neurons (~350) (Aso et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to a previous study on MB anatomy.

claim: Overexpressing CSW in γ neurons showed higher performance with Pro-I when compared with their respective genetic controls.
source: Overexpressing CSW in γ neurons or α/β neurons, but not in α'/β' neurons showed higher performance with Pro-I when compared with their respective genetic controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Overexpressing CSW in α/β neurons showed higher performance with Pro-I when compared with their respective genetic controls.
source: Overexpressing CSW in γ neurons or α/β neurons, but not in α'/β' neurons showed higher performance with Pro-I when compared with their respective genetic controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Overexpressing CSW in α'/β' neurons did not show higher performance with Pro-I when compared with their respective genetic controls.
source: Overexpressing CSW in γ neurons or α/β neurons, but not in α'/β' neurons showed higher performance with Pro-I when compared with their respective genetic controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Acute overexpression of CSW in γ neurons significantly reduced the Pro-I compared with their respective controls.
source: Acute overexpression of CSW in γ neurons (Gal80ts/+; 5-HT1B/UAS-csw, induced), but not in the α/β neurons (C739/+; Gal80ts/UAS-csw, induced), significantly reduced the Pro-I compared with their respective controls (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Acute overexpression of CSW in α/β neurons did not significantly reduce the Pro-I compared with their respective controls.
source: Acute overexpression of CSW in γ neurons (Gal80ts/+; 5-HT1B/UAS-csw, induced), but not in the α/β neurons (C739/+; Gal80ts/UAS-csw, induced), significantly reduced the Pro-I compared with their respective controls (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Acute knockdown of CSW in γ neurons increased the Pro-I.
source: In contrast, acute knockdown of CSW in γ neurons increased the Pro-I (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: CSW regulates Pro-I in MB γ neurons.
source: These data suggest that CSW regulates Pro-I in MB γ neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing CSW effects specifically in γ neurons.

claim: No Pro-I occurred when the two tasks were learned in different contexts.
source: In addition, the result in Figure 1C shows that no Pro-I occurred when the two tasks were learned in different contexts.
evidence: This refers back to experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Knocking down the CSW remained ineffective when the two tasks were learned in different contexts.
source: In this case, knocking down the CSW remained ineffective (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1I.

claim: CSW is generally considered as a positive regulator of Ras/MAPK signaling.
source: CSW is generally considered as a positive regulator of Ras/MAPK signaling (Perkins et al., 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The regulation of CSW on the 'time interval' effect in LTM formation is thought to be via the MAPK pathway.
source: And the regulation of CSW on the 'time interval' effect in LTM formation is also thought to be via the MAPK pathway (Pagani et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Feeding U0126 did not affect single-task learning.
source: Feeding U0126, a widely used inhibitor of the MAPK pathway (Thomas and Huganir, 2004), did not affect single-task learning, but significantly exacerbated Pro-I when learning two consecutive tasks (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Feeding U0126 significantly exacerbated Pro-I when learning two consecutive tasks.
source: Feeding U0126, a widely used inhibitor of the MAPK pathway (Thomas and Huganir, 2004), did not affect single-task learning, but significantly exacerbated Pro-I when learning two consecutive tasks (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Flies with acute genetic knockdown of MAPK in MB neurons exhibited more severe Pro-I than uninduced and parental control flies.
source: Flies with acute genetic knockdown of MAPK in MB neurons (MB-GS/UAS-MAPK-RNAi, RU486+) also exhibited more severe Pro-I than uninduced and parental control flies (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Acute knockdown of Raf significantly exacerbated the Pro-I.
source: Consistent with these results, Raf kinase, a classical upstream regulator of MAPK (Thomas and Huganir, 2004), was found to bidirectionally regulate the Pro-I in MB neurons like CSW (Figure 4C and D). Acutely knocking down Raf significantly exacerbated the Pro-I, while acute overexpression of Raf-GOF, which encodes a constitutively active Raf kinase (Brand and Perrimon, 1994), significantly reduced Pro-I.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Acute overexpression of Raf-GOF significantly reduced Pro-I.
source: Consistent with these results, Raf kinase, a classical upstream regulator of MAPK (Thomas and Huganir, 2004), was found to bidirectionally regulate the Pro-I in MB neurons like CSW (Figure 4C and D). Acutely knocking down Raf significantly exacerbated the Pro-I, while acute overexpression of Raf-GOF, which encodes a constitutively active Raf kinase (Brand and Perrimon, 1994), significantly reduced Pro-I.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Raf kinase is a classical upstream regulator of MAPK.
source: Consistent with these results, Raf kinase, a classical upstream regulator of MAPK (Thomas and Huganir, 2004), was found to bidirectionally regulate the Pro-I in MB neurons like CSW (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Raf-GOF encodes a constitutively active Raf kinase.
source: Acutely knocking down Raf significantly exacerbated the Pro-I, while acute overexpression of Raf-GOF, which encodes a constitutively active Raf kinase (Brand and Perrimon, 1994), significantly reduced Pro-I.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: When Raf-GOF and CSW-RNAi were co-expressed, Raf-GOF expression dominated the effect on Pro-I.
source: When Raf-GOF and CSW-RNAi were co-expressed, Raf-GOF expression dominated the effect on Pro-I, indicating that Raf acts downstream of CSW (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Raf acts downstream of CSW.
source: When Raf-GOF and CSW-RNAi were co-expressed, Raf-GOF expression dominated the effect on Pro-I, indicating that Raf acts downstream of CSW (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is inferred from the epistasis experiment showing Raf-GOF dominates over CSW-RNAi.

claim: CSW regulates Pro-I through Raf/MAPK pathway.
source: Thus, our data support that CSW regulates Pro-I through Raf/MAPK pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing CSW, Raf, and MAPK all regulate Pro-I and their epistatic relationships.

claim: The Raf/MAPK pathway is activated by learning to protect memory retention via non-muscle myosin Ⅱ Sqh after single-task learning.
source: Our previous study found that the Raf/MAPK pathway is activated by learning to protect memory retention via non-muscle myosin Ⅱ Sqh after single-task learning (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement refers to findings from a previous study by the authors.

claim: Manipulating CSW did not affect the learning and memory of a single task.
source: Although the regulatory effect of CSW on Pro-I in two consecutive task learning was also through the Raf/MAPK pathway, manipulating CSW did not affect the learning and memory of a single task (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C), unlike Raf (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Sqh is a downstream molecule of the Raf/MAPK pathway in regulating single-task memory.
source: Interestingly, as a downstream molecule of the Raf/MAPK pathway in regulating single-task memory (Zhang et al., 2018), Sqh did not participate in the Pro-I between the two tasks (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Sqh did not participate in the Pro-I between the two tasks.
source: Interestingly, as a downstream molecule of the Raf/MAPK pathway in regulating single-task memory (Zhang et al., 2018), Sqh did not participate in the Pro-I between the two tasks (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Learning two different tasks consecutively may specifically recruit CSW to activate the Raf/MAPK pathway to reduce Pro-I through downstream molecules different from Sqh.
source: These results suggest that learning two different tasks consecutively may specifically recruit CSW to activate the Raf/MAPK pathway to reduce Pro-I through downstream molecules different from Sqh, a mechanism that differs from the memory protection mechanism triggered by a single learning task.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential roles of CSW and Sqh in two-task vs single-task learning.

claim: The mechanism by which CSW regulates Pro-I differs from the memory protection mechanism triggered by a single learning task.
source: These results suggest that learning two different tasks consecutively may specifically recruit CSW to activate the Raf/MAPK pathway to reduce Pro-I through downstream molecules different from Sqh, a mechanism that differs from the memory protection mechanism triggered by a single learning task.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CSW affects Pro-I but not single-task memory.

claim: In learning two different associative tasks in succession, Pro-I and Retro-I occur simultaneously when the time distance between tasks is close (<20 min).
source: First, in learning two different associative tasks in succession, Pro-I and Retro-I occur simultaneously when the time distance between tasks is close (<20 min), while only Retro-I could be observed when the time distance was far (>20 min).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: Only Retro-I could be observed when the time distance between tasks was far (>20 min).
source: First, in learning two different associative tasks in succession, Pro-I and Retro-I occur simultaneously when the time distance between tasks is close (<20 min), while only Retro-I could be observed when the time distance was far (>20 min).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: The CSW/Raf/MAPK pathway specifically regulates Pro-I.
source: Second, we identify a molecular pathway that specifically regulates Pro-I: the CSW/Raf/MAPK pathway.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 3 and 4 showing this pathway regulates Pro-I but not Retro-I or single-task learning.

claim: The upstream signaling molecule CSW of this pathway is not involved in single-task learning and memory.
source: The upstream signaling molecule CSW of this pathway is not involved in single-task learning and memory.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: In learning two different tasks close in time, although Pro-I and Retro-I occurred simultaneously, CSW was only involved in regulating Pro-I.
source: In learning two different tasks close in time, although Pro-I and Retro-I occurred simultaneously, CSW was only involved in regulating Pro-I.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3F showing CSW does not affect Retro-I.

claim: Rac1 specifically regulates Retro-I without affecting Pro-I when two different tasks are temporally close.
source: Third, Rac1 specifically regulates Retro-I without affecting Pro-I when two different tasks are temporally close.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2F.

claim: The Rac1/SCAR/Dia pathway has been reported to regulate Retro-I when the two tasks are temporally distant (1.5 hr interval).
source: Consistently, the Rac1/SCAR/Dia pathway has been reported to regulate Retro-I when the two tasks are temporally distant (1.5 hr interval) (Gao et al., 2019; Shuai et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: After 20 min, the memory performance of the proactive task partially declines and a consolidated memory component called anesthesia-resistant memory (ARM) is largely formed.
source: After 20 min, the memory performance of the proactive task partially declines and a consolidated memory component called anesthesia-resistant memory (ARM) is largely formed (Quinn and Dudai, 1976; Tully et al., 1994; Tully and Quinn, 1985; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies on memory dynamics.

claim: The decay or consolidation of the proactive task may release Pro-I.
source: It raises a possibility that the decay or consolidation of the proactive task may release Pro-I.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the temporal dynamics of Pro-I and memory consolidation.

claim: Acute knockdown or overexpression of CSW in MB neurons did not affect the immediate and early memory performance of a single task.
source: First, acute knockdown or overexpression of CSW in MB neurons did not affect the immediate and early memory performance of a single task (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: In the Retro-I paradigm, the proactive task in the Pro-I paradigm became the target task and was directly examined, however, its performance was not affected by manipulating CSW.
source: Second, in the Retro-I paradigm, the proactive task in the Pro-I paradigm became the target task and was directly examined, however, its performance was not affected by manipulating CSW (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Manipulating Raf/MAPK pathway in MB neurons during the adult stage did not affect immediate memory and ARM performance after a single aversive learning task.
source: Third, manipulating Raf/MAPK pathway in MB neurons during the adult stage did not affect immediate memory and ARM performance after a single aversive learning task (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Inter-task similarity from different dimensions contributes to Pro-I.
source: Our current findings suggest that inter-task similarity from different dimensions contributes to Pro-I.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results in Figure 1 showing effects of content, context, and temporal similarity.

claim: The content similarity between tasks can influence Pro-I.
source: First, the content similarity between tasks can influence Pro-I.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Two similar aversive associative tasks could produce significant Pro-I.
source: Two similar aversive associative tasks could produce significant Pro-I.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1A.

claim: Pro-I was not observed after reducing the inter-task content similarity by replacing the proactive task with non-associative stimuli or an appetitive associative task.
source: However, Pro-I was not observed after reducing the inter-task content similarity by replacing the proactive task with non-associative stimuli or an appetitive associative task (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Due to the similarity of content, both tasks are more likely to use the same neural circuit thus increasing the possibility of Pro-I.
source: Due to the similarity of content, both tasks are more likely to use the same neural circuit thus increasing the possibility of Pro-I.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference about why content similarity affects Pro-I.

claim: The similarity of environmental contexts between tasks plays an important role in Pro-I.
source: Second, the similarity of environmental contexts between tasks plays an important role in Pro-I.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1C.

claim: Pro-I was significantly released when the similarity of environmental contexts between tasks was reduced.
source: Pro-I was significantly released when the similarity of environmental contexts between tasks was reduced (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The similarity of time contexts between tasks also contributes to Pro-I.
source: Third, the similarity of time contexts between tasks also contributes to Pro-I.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2 showing ITI effects.

claim: Time is considered as a context.
source: Time is also considered as a context (Bouton, 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: When the ITI was increased to more than 20 min, the Pro-I is no longer significant.
source: When the ITI was increased to more than 20 min, the Pro-I is no longer significant (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: The 20 min ITI might make the time contexts of the two tasks significantly different, thus reducing the inter-task similarity.
source: This phenomenon can be explained as the 20 min ITI might make the time contexts of the two tasks significantly different, thus reducing the inter-task similarity.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the ITI effect on Pro-I.

claim: The CSW/Raf/MAPK pathway can regulate Pro-I probably by affecting time context similarity between tasks.
source: According to this explanation, the CSW/Raf/MAPK pathway can regulate Pro-I probably by affecting time context similarity between tasks.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis about how CSW/Raf/MAPK regulates Pro-I.

claim: Aversive learning can induce MAPK activation that peaks at around 20 min, which can be modulated by CSW and Raf.
source: Aversive learning can induce MAPK activation that peaks at around 20 min, which can be modulated by CSW and Raf (Pagani et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Overexpression of CSW in MB neurons is reported to accelerate MAPK activation.
source: Overexpression of CSW in MB neurons is reported to accelerate MAPK activation (Pagani et al., 2009) and can reduce Pro-I (Figure 3D, E and H).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Knocking down Raf in MB neurons shortens the duration of MAPK activation.
source: Knocking down Raf in MB neurons shortens the duration of MAPK activation (Zhang et al., 2018) and can exacerbate Pro-I (Figure 4C).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: MAPK activation can help distinguish the time contexts of the two tasks.
source: With these findings, an interesting idea is that MAPK activation can help distinguish the time contexts of the two tasks.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the mechanism by which MAPK affects Pro-I.

claim: The CSW/Raf/MAPK pathway can bidirectionally regulate Pro-I by affecting the similarity of time contexts between tasks.
source: Thus, the CSW/Raf/MAPK pathway can bidirectionally regulate Pro-I by affecting the similarity of time contexts between tasks.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis synthesizing the experimental findings.

claim: The properties of Pro-I obtained using the Drosophila model are consistent with psychological studies.
source: These properties of Pro-I that we obtained using the Drosophila model are consistent with psychological studies (Kliegl and Bäuml, 2021).
evidence: This statement compares current findings to previous psychological literature.

claim: Pro-I in the current work only occurs when the interval between two tasks is less than 20 min.
source: Although Pro-I in the current work only occurs when the interval between two tasks is less than 20 min, the phenomenon of Pro-I varies across biological learning systems and tasks (Crossley et al., 2019; Epp et al., 2016; Jonides and Nee, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2 and citations to literature showing variability.

claim: The phenomenon of Pro-I varies across biological learning systems and tasks.
source: Although Pro-I in the current work only occurs when the interval between two tasks is less than 20 min, the phenomenon of Pro-I varies across biological learning systems and tasks (Crossley et al., 2019; Epp et al., 2016; Jonides and Nee, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The molecules regulating Pro-I and Retro-I in Drosophila are involved in different diseases with varying levels of intellectual disability.
source: Interestingly, the molecules regulating Pro-I and Retro-I in Drosophila are involved in different diseases with varying levels of intellectual disability.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent statements about Rac1, Fmr1, and PTPN11 in disease.

claim: Rac1 and Fmr1, which regulate Retro-I in Drosophila, are high-risk genes for autism.
source: Rac1 and Fmr1, which regulate Retro-I in Drosophila, are high-risk genes for autism (Lord et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature on autism genetics.

claim: Mutations in PTPN11, a human orthologue of csw, account for more than half of Noonan syndrome.
source: Mutations in PTPN11, a human orthologue of csw, account for more than half of Noonan syndrome (Roberts et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature on Noonan syndrome.

claim: Further studies on the molecular mechanisms underlying Pro-I and Retro-I may contribute to the understanding of the pathogenesis of autism and Noonan syndrome.
source: Therefore, further studies on the molecular mechanisms underlying Pro-I and Retro-I may also contribute to the understanding of the pathogenesis of autism and Noonan syndrome.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential translational relevance of the findings.

claim: Studies of Pro-I and Retro-I from the synaptic and neural circuit levels may inspire continual learning in artificial intelligence.
source: In addition, studies of Pro-I and Retro-I from the synaptic and neural circuit levels may also inspire continual learning in artificial intelligence (Wang et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculation about potential applications supported by citations.

claim: Flies were cultured at 23℃ and 60% relative humidity with standard medium under a 12 hr light-dark cycle.
source: Flies (Drosophila melanogaster) were cultured at 23℃ and 60% relative humidity with standard medium under a 12 hr light-dark cycle.
evidence: This is a methodological description of experimental conditions.

claim: MB-GS was a gift from Dr. Ronald L. Davis.
source: MB-GS was a gift from Dr. Ronald L. Davis (Mao et al., 2004).
evidence: This describes the source of a reagent with citation.

claim: The insertion site of UAS-csw in the transgenic line (#23878) acquired from Bloomington Stock Center is the X chromosome.
source: Since the insertion site of UAS-csw in the transgenic line (#23878) acquired from Bloomington Storck Center is the X chromosome, a distinction between male and female flies needs to be made when counting behavioral results.
evidence: This is a methodological consideration based on the genetic properties of the fly line.

claim: A new transgenic strain (UAS-csw, insertion on chromosome III) was constructed for experimental convenience.
source: For experimental convenience, we constructed a new transgenic strain (UAS-csw, insertion on chromosome III) and used it mainly in this study.
evidence: This describes a methodological approach taken in the study.
